messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob!

What happened was that the CVODE library got swapped out for the CVODES library. Since the CVODES library is source compatible to CVODE client code this worked without any change to the integrate_ode_cvode function which has been in math and is unchanged.

Let's discuss during the meeting, but I would actually suggest to change the name of the function integrate_ode_cvode to integrate_ode_bdf before we tag. We could possibly do this in the language stan? This is just an idea in order to avoid having a growing list of function names to deprecate.

In 2.11 we would then change the implementation of the cvode integrator to the one which is currently under review - and things would only get faster, no other change.

I hope the design of the CVODES branch I wrote is now as everyone agreed to in their minds.

Sebastian

@ Ben: For rstan CVODES will be distributed, so we won't have to change anything there in the future. However, could you please double-check that all printf statements are ifdefed-out. I mean when changing to CVODES, I took over the patches you had put into CVODE, but please have a final look to make sure that CVODES did not introduce more. Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [stan-users] Numerical Problems in MCMC Metropolis Simulation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] [stan-users] Numerical Problems in MCMC Metropolis Simulation
messages.body_plain:
This is all addressed in the integration time paper.

To briefly summarize, let theta_{0} be the initial
point and let ( \theta_{0}, \ldots, \theta_{N} ) be
an ensemble of proposals including the initial
point.

There are numerous ways of choosing a point
from this ensemble while maintaining the correct
invariant distribution.

We could multinomially sample each point using the weights

p( theta_{n} ) = pi( theta_{n} ) / ( sum_{m = 0}^{N} pi( theta_{m} )

Or we could slice sample by sampling a threshold

u \sim U(0, \pi(theta_{0} )

and then uniformly sample from the points in the
ensemble with densities above this threshold,

theta_{new} \sim U( theta_{n} | pi(theta_{n}) > u ).

Both of these procedures generate leave the exact
target distribution invariant, and hence when applied
to HMC exactly correct for any error in the symplectic
integrator.

~ Charles

messages.subject: an idea for some warning messages
messages.subject_clean: an idea for some warning messages
messages.body_plain:
There are some distributions that we (that is, I) just about never like in a Stan model:
- hard constraints that do not correspond to actual boundaries of parameter space
- inverse-gamma priors with low degrees of freedom
- parameters with super-wide priors such as normal(0,1000)
- uniform distributions
We can probably think of a few more.

Anyway, I’m wondering if the parser should include an option (which by default would be on) to spit out warnings when some of these things are detected.
I can come up with a specific proposal if there is interest.  Some natural flags would be upper and lower bounds that are not 0 or 1, inverse-gamma with parameters set to fixed values less than 1, normals with fixed sd’s higher than 100, any uniform distributions, parameters with names that begin with “sigma” that do not have <lower=0>, etc.
Again, just warnings, not errors, and there should be a way to turn the warnings off if it irritates people, but I think this could make a big difference!

A

messages.subject: integrate_ode functions for v2.10
messages.body_plain:
I wanted some confirmation that this is the right thing to do.

1) In stan-dev/math, we will have two functions (more later):
  - integrate_ode_rk45 (used to be called integrate_ode in v2.9)
  - integrate_ode_bdf (use to be called integrate_ode_cvode, but not in any tagged version)

2) In stan-dev/stan, we will have four functions (more later):
  - integrate_ode. This will call integrate_ode_rk45 in the math library.
  - integrate_ode_rk45. There will be two function signatures and both will call integrate_ode_rk45 in the math library.
  - integrate_ode_stiff. This will call integrate_ode_bdf in the math library.
  - integrate_ode_bdf. There will be two function signatures and both will call integrate_ode_bdf in the math library.

The above is how I'm approaching the fix.

The alternative is to have functions in the math library called integrate_ode and integrate_ode_stiff that the language calls directly. I'll have a patch out for review soon.

Daniel

messages.subject: Edward: (another) library for probabilistic modeling, inference, and criticism
messages.subject_clean: Edward: (another) library for probabilistic modeling, inference, and criticism
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

Just wanted to let you know that a few of us in Dave Blei's group have released a Python library (https://github.com/blei-lab/edward) a few days ago, which does variational inference among other things.

We were motivated primarily by research: there's a lack of software in the machine learning community for developing new probability models and inference algorithms. While Bayesian practices (and more generally, statistical practices) in machine learning is rising, it is by far a minority in the field. I think part of this reason is because of the lack of software to readily apply these tools, where a student may not have the foresight to see how a hierarchical linear model connects to an SVM or neural network. We hope to bridge this gap by appealing to deep learners with ""state-of-the-art"" results for example while pointing them to foundational questions such as validating their models and inference.

Also I'd like to dispel any potential misunderstandings: the software distinguishes itself from Stan by first and foremost being a library for methodological research rather than a library for applied research. This means that we're leveraging a lot of the recent tools such as TensorFlow as the backend for GPU support and computational graphs, data subsampling, BBVI for discrete latent variable models and Bayesian nonparametric models, and neural network tools for composing deep generative models. To do this we sacrifice a lot of the robustness and stability that Stan does well. After the research has matured—just like how Rayleigh has a tool for benchmarking inference algorithms—then we can think about how to put it into Stan.

Dustin

>
> We were motivated primarily by research: there's a lack of software in the machine learning community for developing new probability models and inference algorithms. While Bayesian practices (and more generally, statistical practices) in machine learning is rising, it is by far a minority in the field. I think part of this reason is because of the lack of software to readily apply these tools, where a student may not have the foresight to see how a hierarchical linear model connects to an SVM or neural network. We hope to bridge this gap by appealing to deep learners with ""state-of-the-art"" results for example while pointing them to foundational questions such as validating their models and inference.
>
> Also I'd like to dispel any potential misunderstandings: the software distinguishes itself from Stan by first and foremost being a library for methodological research rather than a library for applied research. This means that we're leveraging a lot of the recent tools such as TensorFlow as the backend for GPU support and computational graphs, data subsampling, BBVI for discrete latent variable models and Bayesian nonparametric models, and neural network tools for composing deep generative models. To do this we sacrifice a lot of the robustness and stability that Stan does well. After the research has matured—just like how Rayleigh has a tool for benchmarking inference algorithms—then we can think about how to put it into Stan.
>
> Dustin

Here’s what we had to write to get distributions in TensorFlow:

https://github.com/blei-lab/edward/blob/master/edward/stats/distributions.py

It’s very bare bones. The log density only supports scalar arguments with limited support for vectorized arguments. The random number generation also resorts to SciPy, which is not very useful for TensorFlow because it doesn’t work well with the symbolic computations. The current hack, without using Stan math, is to build our own random number generation from TensorFlow’s uniform sampler: https://github.com/blei-lab/edward/issues/51. You can see how much reinventing the wheel there is.

Dustin

messages.subject: integrate_ode_rk45 - expose step_size?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I was just going through the integrate_ode_rk45 and found that the initial step_size gets exposed as an option. I thought we only expose abs+rel tol and max_num_steps, but not step_size, no?

The step_size gets automatically adjusted by the rk45 algorithm according to abs+rel tolerance specifications. To me it would make sense to export step_size if we were to expose rk4 which uses a fixed step size all the time, but the initial step size should not matter performance wise for the rk45 (ok, up to an epsilon).

Maybe I was wrong in my understanding of what we decided.

Best,
Sebastian

Isn't 32-bit floating point dangerous from a precision point
of view?  Is it there because it's more amenable to GPU parallelization?

How does the GPU integration work with Python code like this?

Are function calls so expensive in Python that you can't pull
out all the cut-and-paste code like the RHS of these:

        x = tf.cast(tf.squeeze(x), dtype=tf.float32)
        a = tf.cast(tf.squeeze(a), dtype=tf.float32)
        b = tf.cast(tf.squeeze(b), dtype=tf.float32)

Does Python have anything like pass-by-reference?  If so, then
you could write all these as single functions.

I would strongly recommend putting the operators first on a newline
C++/Java-style rather than at the end R-style.  That \ at the end
of lines is the price you pay for no semicolons or brackets;  nothing
to be done about that.

Also, there's a lot you can do to optimize all this code by rearranging
terms.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cvodes_integrator feedback?
messages.body_plain:
Firstly, a reminder that moving forward we should use more descriptive branch names,
at least not having mysterious numerical labels! Something like “refactor_integrate_ode”
would be appropriate here, and the branch name can be changed so don’t hesitate to
do so before a pull request.

ode_system.hpp

Line 14: No reason to have abbreviations in comments.

Line 15: “S” and “P” aren’t used in this implementation, no need to define them.

Line 21: If it’s got methods, it’s a class.  Just style.

Line 57, 76, etc:  Qualitifers/types on same line.  So “inline void” instead of “inline\nvoid”

integrate_ode_bdf.hpp

Line 32: No abbreviations.  This is worth a few sentences.

Line 87: I recommend breaking this line to

cvodes_integrator<F, T_initial, T_param>
  integrator(f, y0, t0,…

to free up lots of vertical space.

cvodes_integrator.hpp

Line 44: Why is ts_ a member variable?  It’s used only in integrate and would be better
              left as an argument to that method.

Line 45 - 47: N, M, and S need to be doc’d.

Line 177:  Split this up into two if/then and move the common code in between, as in

if (solver == 0)
 cvode_mem_ = CVodeCreate(CV_ADAMS, CV_FUNCTIONAL);
else
 cvode_mem_ = CVodeCreate(CV_BDF, CV_NEWTON);

  if (cvode_mem_ == NULL)
    throw std::runtime_error("CVodeCreate failed to allocate memory”);

  set_cvode_options(rel_tol, abs_tol, max_num_steps);

   if (solver != 0) {
          // for the stiff solvers we need to reserve additional
          // memory and provide a Jacobian function call
          check_flag(CVDense(cvode_mem_, N_), "CVDense");
          check_flag(CVDlsSetDenseJacFn(cvode_mem_, &solver::dense_jacobian),
                      "CVDlsSetDenseJacFn");
    }

   if (solver == 2)
            check_flag(CVodeSetStabLimDet(cvode_mem_, 1), "CVodeSetStabLimDet”);

Note sure if "set_cvode_options(rel_tol, abs_tol, max_num_steps);” needs to be
factored into its own function as it would be called only once, but not a big deal
either way.

Line 214: I don’t think you need the braces, but not critical to remove them.

Line 252: Why cast to a solver const pointer?  Did you mean const solver?

Line 312+: Can’t all of these methods be moved into ode_system, and then
pass a pointer to the ode_system implementation in CVodeSetUserData?
I think that’s the more natural factoring here.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Unicode characters in variable names
messages.body_plain:
Sorry to revive an old (but recent) thread. In Julia, I have been staying away from Unicode variable names for a while, being concerned about font support, editor support, and corrupted files. And frankly, the whole thing looked like a gimmick.

Then I have tried and within a few days I changed my opinion completely. I find that I can organize my code better, and use variable names that are short yet correspond to formulas in papers. This leads to very compact equations. Corruption has not been a problem in practice (using UTF8 all the time).

AFAIK most editors support some form of entry. In Emacs for example, you can use autocomplete, company-mode, and quail (see eg the packages listed at the end of https://github.com/vspinu/math-symbol-lists ) to enter \alpha for α. So it would be great to have Unicode in Stan.

Best,

Tamas

> If you do want to do this at some point, the way that Julia handles is (apart from arbitrary operators) seems like a good set of rules:
>
>
> Variable names must begin with a letter (A-Z or a-z), underscore, or a subset of Unicode code points greater than 00A0; in particular, Unicode character categories Lu/Ll/Lt/Lm/Lo/Nl (letters), Sc/So (currency and other symbols), and a few other letter-like characters (e.g. a subset of the Sm math symbols) are allowed. Subsequent characters may also include ! and digits (0-9 and other characters in categories Nd/No), as well as other Unicode code points: diacritics and other modifying marks (categories Mn/Mc/Me/Sk), some punctuation connectors (category Pc), primes, and a few other characters.
>
>  Operators like + are also valid identifiers, but are parsed specially. In some contexts, operators can be used just like variables; for example (+) refers to the addition function, and (+) = f will reassign it. Most of the Unicode infix operators (in category Sm), such as ⊕, are parsed as infix operators and are available for user-defined methods (e.g. you can use const ⊗ = kron to define⊗ as an infix Kronecker product).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cvodes_integrator feedback?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Thanks for your comments. Let me answer inline…

> Am 08.05.2016 um 17:07 schrieb Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>:
>
> Firstly, a reminder that moving forward we should use more descriptive branch names,
> at least not having mysterious numerical labels! Something like “refactor_integrate_ode”
> would be appropriate here, and the branch name can be changed so don’t hesitate to
> do so before a pull request.

Well, the CVODES stuff is getting a (long) history. I can rename, but then we loose the current pull request

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/pull/283

And the comments there were good, I think. Let’s quickly touch base tomorrow if we want to start from scratch with a new name and a new pull.

>
> ode_system.hpp
>
> Line 14: No reason to have abbreviations in comments.
>
> Line 15: “S” and “P” aren’t used in this implementation, no need to define them.
>
> Line 21: If it’s got methods, it’s a class.  Just style.
>
> Line 57, 76, etc:  Qualitifers/types on same line.  So “inline void” instead of “inline\nvoid”

Thanks. Some comments still described old design (the abbreviations); I adapted this and tried to follow those style rules as I assume these are standard in Stan.

>
> integrate_ode_bdf.hpp
>
> Line 32: No abbreviations.  This is worth a few sentences.
>
> Line 87: I recommend breaking this line to
>
>
> cvodes_integrator<F, T_initial, T_param>
>  integrator(f, y0, t0,…
>
> to free up lots of vertical space.

Ok, done.

>
> cvodes_integrator.hpp
>
> Line 44: Why is ts_ a member variable?  It’s used only in integrate and would be better
>              left as an argument to that method.

I would prefer to leave it where it is. It belongs together with y0 and t0, I think. Moreover, we may want to revisit at some point the initial step size of cvode - it sets the initial step size based an a scary guess of y’’ and it is nowhere documented how this is done. So maybe we would like to set the initial step-size when configuring cvode in the constructor based on a scan through ts at some point.

>
> Line 45 - 47: N, M, and S need to be doc’d.
>

Sure. I add some notes for other bookkeeping ints as well.

> Line 177:  Split this up into two if/then and move the common code in between, as in
>
>
> if (solver == 0)
> cvode_mem_ = CVodeCreate(CV_ADAMS, CV_FUNCTIONAL);
> else
> cvode_mem_ = CVodeCreate(CV_BDF, CV_NEWTON);
>
>  if (cvode_mem_ == NULL)
>    throw std::runtime_error("CVodeCreate failed to allocate memory”);
>
>  set_cvode_options(rel_tol, abs_tol, max_num_steps);
>
>   if (solver != 0) {
>          // for the stiff solvers we need to reserve additional
>          // memory and provide a Jacobian function call
>          check_flag(CVDense(cvode_mem_, N_), "CVDense");
>          check_flag(CVDlsSetDenseJacFn(cvode_mem_, &solver::dense_jacobian),
>                      "CVDlsSetDenseJacFn");
>    }
>
>   if (solver == 2)
>            check_flag(CVodeSetStabLimDet(cvode_mem_, 1), "CVodeSetStabLimDet”);
>
> Note sure if "set_cvode_options(rel_tol, abs_tol, max_num_steps);” needs to be
> factored into its own function as it would be called only once, but not a big deal
> either way.
>

Your proposal is very close to what I had before. Daniel and Bob found it to be preferable to have a single if/then/else - as such a set_cvode_option function makes a lot of sense. I am leaving it for the moment as is, since this way of writing was seen as a step forward.

> Line 214: I don’t think you need the braces, but not critical to remove them.

Yes, they are not needed, but actually I prefer them to write them one time too often rather than forgetting.

>
> Line 252: Why cast to a solver const pointer?  Did you mean const solver?

const applies to what is on the left as I learned recently (and only to the right if nothing is left of it); I changed to const solver if that is more natural to read.

>
> Line 312+: Can’t all of these methods be moved into ode_system, and then
> pass a pointer to the ode_system implementation in CVodeSetUserData?
> I think that’s the more natural factoring here.

The intent of the design is to keep all C related code inside cvodes_integrator such that we have a single point where this interface to the C library happens. Moreover, having ode_system like it is now will allow us to (i) refactor the coupled_ode_system object using ode_system and (ii) have a straightforward way to supply analytic Jacobians to our ODE solvers using partial template specialization. I hope this makes sense to you, I believe Bob and Daniel came to agree to this approach.

In the meantime I added tests for the decouple_ode_states and the ode_system object. I hope those tests are inline with the overall testing strategy.

Thanks again for looking.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
Okay, hopefully the last big change has been pushed: http://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro.

The biggest change was an expanded discussion of propositional logic that completely
motivates measure and probability theory.  Ultimately this is an introduction to measure/
probability theory, only without the usually mathematical pedantry and a much stronger
motivation from logic as a means of describing arbitrary systems.  I also set up the
measure-theoretic version of Bayes’ Theorem from the beginning, again motivated
by logic, which makes the construction of Bayesian inference super easy.

I’m sure some of the notation can be cleaned up, and I’m happy to add more exposition
(or even exercises at some point?) if anyone finds sections particularly esoteric or
hard to read, but overall I think this is the level of detail that is necessary to really
understand what’s going on.

Once again, any and all comments are welcome.

On Apr 1, 2016, at 7:26 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The manuscript has been significantly updated and expanded,
> https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
>
> On Mar 17, 2016, at 11:47 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> One of the common problems that we keep running into is that
>> everyone has different, and usually incomplete, understandings
>> of probability.  Of course probability theory is relatively abstract
>> and we’re not going to be able to teach it to those without
>> reasonable math backgrounds: in that case the approaches
>> of McElreath and Kruschke are probably best.  What doesn’t
>> exist in the literature is an introductory treatment of probability
>> theory and inference that goes into all of the technical details
>> for those who do have a reasonable math background.  I’m
>> talking about concepts like concentration of measure, the
>> difference between probability, probability mass functions,
>> and probability density function.
>>
>> Anyways, I think we’re going to need a treatment like that
>> in the Stan manual going forward, and this is my best
>> attempt at an initial draft, https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
>> Conditioned on a familiarity with calculus everything should,
>> hopefully, be self-contained and well-defined.
>>
>> The inference section is still a little bit in flux, but I’m really
>> happy about the general organization of the probability sections.
>> That said, I’m sure there are many topics that unclear or
>> too hastily introduced or could use more examples to build
>> intuition, so let me have it.  Either here on the list or via an
>> issue/PR.  Otherwise let me know what you think.
>

messages.subject: Re: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
Thank you creating this technical introduction: very stimulating and enlightening!

I find section 4 challenging, so I'm sharing my thoughts in the hope of getting some clarification, and pointing out a concept other readers might struggle with. I am having a hard time with Concentration of Measure, particularly the fact the neighborhood we want to explore does not include the mode in the hyper-sphere example.

So here's what I get: the volume element is proportional to r^(D-1), so dV increases as we move away from the origin, which is where the mode is. Consequently, the PMF is NOT concentrated at the origin but at a certain shell. This is clearly illustrated in figure 4.2 (I would consider rewriting the equations for dV and PDF in the figure's description). From a "markov chain point of view" this is telling me that the vast majority of the parameters I want to include in my sample are located in the "typical set shell". If I only stick around the mode, I will get the parameters with the highest PDF, but most of the mass will be lost, and my final sample will be unrepresentative.

Ok -- so if I were to pick the most "massive" shell, it would certainly not be located at the origin. But why am I constrained to pick a shell? If instead of picking a shell, I were picking a finite volume to do my exploration in, wouldn't the most massive volume include the origin of the sphere (and maybe part of the typical set shell)? So the key question is why do I need to pick a shell, instead of a volume, which to me is what only exploring the typical set seems to imply.

My tentative answer is that it takes computational power for a markov chain to move around the parameter space. But I am then unsure how exploring the entire typical set shell ends up being less costly than moving to the center of the sphere and out of it again.

Any clarification would be welcome!

~ Charles

Any evaluations near the mode don’t contribute to any expectation
and so are wasted.  You are welcome to include them, but will
pay a significant computational cost to do so.

messages.subject: _rng in transformed data block
messages.body_plain:
I've been writing some scripts for ODSC Boston that simulate data using model parameters or the generated quantities block.  The manual says the _rng functions can only be used in generated quantities but it would be nice to simulate some discrete values and then use the model block to simulate from a relevant posterior.  I guess for simple models I can pack everything into the generated quantities section but that won't work if I want to simulate from something more complex (e.g.-inhomogeneous poisson process with a smooth intensity function).

The question here is whether this is straightforward but we don't have time for it or whether there's a deeper reason we're not doing it.  Sorry for the barrage of simple questions but I've been exercising Stan usage more than usual for this workshop.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: example of what I meant on what to doc
messages.subject_clean: example of what I meant on what to doc
messages.body_plain: Andrew mentioned that I'm against certain kinds of doc. I'm doing some code review and thought I'd provide everyone some examples. One of those types is repeating what's in the code and documenting the language, both of which Google's style guide for C++ warns against. This example I just found in the code does both: * ... The autodiff-based implementation for * reverse-mode are defined in namespace stan::math * and may be invoked via argument-dependent lookup by including * their headers. The namespace declarations cover the first, and ADL is just part of the language. What I said is that you should doc things that go against standard language idioms and best practices, usually hacks to deal with some external interface or efficiency issue. Here's an example of something that should be documented by better variable naming (N_state_size) or just not at all (given that y0 is documented as the state already, and size() is just size of containers) // number of states const size_t N = y0.size(); I'm also not keen on these, but I can live with them: } // math } // stan And just so you don't think I'm saying don't use code comments at all, this is the kind of thing that's useful: // initialize forward sensitivity system of CVODES as needed It's documenting the purpose of a block of code. It'd be even better to break the block into a function named something like initialize_forward_sensitivity(...). Then it's self-documnenting and the code's more modular. In almost all cases, a block of code longer than a screenful should be broken up into functions (and lest you think I'm well behaved myself, see lang/generator.hpp for a big dose of "do what I say, not what I do"). I'm not trying to pick on a particular file or author, just using this to explain what I meant (and by the way, the file I got these from has beautiful API doc and is mostly broken up into utility function calls with descriptive names). Just to repeat, I'm a very strong proponent of writing doxygen-style doc for each function. That's what defines the interfaces, lays out what should be tested, and lets external users use your function without understanding all its details. That is, encapsulation of implementation, from which almost all good flows in computer system design. I wrote a blog post on this a while ago at: https://lingpipe-blog.com/2009/10/15/the-futility-of-commenting-code/ People always say nobody does this, hence the examples above and https://lingpipe-blog.com/2009/10/19/examples-of-futility-of-commenting-cod/ - Bob

Hi all,

I'm back! The code is complete without any optimization of the gradients. Before it's ready, it needs the tests Seth mentioned.

Seth and everyone else, writing tests isn't about C++ code. It's all about being willing to be careful and do a little bit of work. If all you did was in a document put down inputs and outputs, then coding those are trivial. It's generating enough test cases and the combinations under which we would instantiate the code that matters.

The reason I want this to be well tested first is we will want to make this faster. Once we get into the territory of writing custom derivative code for operators, it is immensely helpful to have existing tests that we know work. It's really hard to get code right the first time.

Seth forwarded the analytic gradients (sorry -- I meant to forward that to the list, but I sat on it). What we should do is in any format you want (but a test is best), write out:
- input. Something like: (x data = [1, 2, 3], sigma data = 1, lambda data = 1), (x var = [1, 2, 3], sigma var = 1, lambda var = 1)
- output. Something like: cov_mat = [3x3 matrix], dcov_mat[1,1] / d_x[1] = ?, dcov_mat[1,2] / d_x[2] = ?, ..., dcov_mat[1,1] / d_sigma, ...

And we have to hit the edge cases. So... sigma = 0. lambda = 0. sigma = inf...

I have a few more high priority things going on. I've tested it a little bit, but we need more tests. If you want to help, just write down sets of input and output and we can code that into tests easily. Would it help if I put in a skeleton test to show you how it's done? I don't know how much more I can do to get those that are interested in just writing down test cases.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] finishing a covariance function implementation (for GPs)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] finishing a covariance function implementation (for GPs)
messages.body_plain:
I think what we really want down the road is
a function that returns the Cholesky decomposition
of the covariance matrix directly, and at that point
we could wrap everything up in a single (matrix-valued)
node on the expression graph, no?

The nice feature of this design is that if we get
structured covariance matrices then we can use
structured solvers behind the scenes (once we have
support for structured solvers, etc…)

On May 24, 2016, at 11:21 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> On Tuesday, May 24, 2016 at 3:43:20 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> On May 23, 2016, at 4:04 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>>>
>>> On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 5:13:19 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>> Devin doesn't know C++ yet and this one's hairy or Daniel would be
>>>> done with already.  All these higher-order tests are also what's
>>>> bogging down the vectorization.
>>>
>>> And my guess is that with enough functions vectorized, the covariance matrix computation could be fully vectorized when written in Stan language so that the expression tree would be smallish and it would be quite fast even without internal C++ implementation of the covariance function...
>>
>> But the current vectorization of functions doesn't cut
>> down expression tree size --- it's just a loop on the
>> inside of the function instead of int he Stan language,
>> which doesn't matter for efficiency.
>
> Oh :(
> Thanks for pointing this out.
>
> Aki
>
>>
>> The vectorized distributions are another matter --- those
>> do create just one new node (with an edge to each input --- the
>> complexity is a multiply-add per edge, and also a virtual function
>> call for each node).
>>
>> - Bob
>

"quad" and "cov" elsewhere.

messages.subject: serialization format for MCMC & metadata format?
messages.subject_clean: serialization format for MCMC & metadata format?
messages.body_plain:
The discussion about PyStan about bringing together
chains runs separately brings up a good issue.

We've been talking about C++ API-level interfaces, but
not about any kind of serialization format.

The current CSV output from CmdStan is a CSV file
for parameters and draws, with a lot of added metadata
in comments, including adaptation information and settings
for how CmdStan was run.

It'd be nice to settle on something like a simple CSV
format like this for draws.  It's a bit of a hack now because
array indexing is done by name-mangling in the header.

We could compress the files to save space.

But that leaves a serialization format for all the metadata.
And for adaptation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] PyStan output
messages.body_plain:
Another reason to support a serialized output is to cut
down on memory contention between the draws and the sampler.
If you run the sampler, dump to file, then read back in,
then the peak memory requirements are much lower.

I think it makes sense to split PyStan into two parts.
One that just wraps Stan and produces output and one
that reads in MCMC output and analyzes it.  ShinyStan and
other packages like Loo are doing some of that output
analysis for us on the R side.  So there's a lot to coordinate!

- Bob

messages.subject: nested key:value in config?
messages.body_plain:
In the past we've had some arguments about whether to allow nesting in the configuration specification and I wanted to see if it would fly now (in the configuration output).  I'm in favor of that since it makes it easier to specify names (in the style of CmdStan command line) so that they don't conflict among algorithms.  For example, the style in the _current_ output is:

 algorithm = lbfgs (Default)
       lbfgs
         init_alpha = 0.001 (Default)
         tol_obj = 9.9999999999999998e-13 (Default)
         tol_rel_obj = 10000 (Default)
         tol_grad = 1e-08 (Default)

Where the meaning of init_alpha is unambiguous because it's nested in lbfgs but another algorithm might have an init_alpha with a completely different meaning.  It also makes the config output order-independent since you don't have to search for the algorithm:bfgs key-value pair before you know what init_alpha:0.001 key-value pair means.

We'll have another go at this when it's code rather than spec but if you have any fundamental objections I'd appreciate hearing them now. (or suggestions).

Krzysztof

One goal is just recordkeeping to record how a sample
was gathered.  For that, human readability is a big help.

each interface will need to read at least some of the
information back in.  For that, we need parsers in each
language.

If the readers for nested structures are manageable,
I'd be OK with nesting.

I'd like the output that gets dumped to be human readable
if at all possible.  The reason is so

  * we don't have to maintain two tools (human readable and binary)

  * the two versions (human readable and binary) won't get out of synch

  * there'll never be a translator of binary to human readable of
    the wrong version

The more data-like stuff I'm happier to put in a binary format,
but even then, there's a big advantage to something like CSV.
Rarely is the I/O the bottleneck (though it certainly can be with
really fast systems with lots of data, like big data optimization
problems).

>> Another goal is to be able to restart.  To restart,
>> each interface will need to read at least some of the
>> information back in.  For that, we need parsers in each
>> language.

> rely on something that's broadly used like JSON/protobuf/etc...
>
>> If the readers for nested structures are manageable,
>
> I don't even know how to answer that question without just
> implementing it in C++ and seeing what API I can produce
> for interfaces...

That's the Catch-22 of designing computer programs.

- Bob

On 05/31, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> CSV is also waaaaaay easier to use with Unix tools.

I haven't found this to be true in my work. I always have to use Python
(pandas) or R to read CSV files because there's frequently some
idiosyncrasy in the CSV file, which we should expect since CSV isn't a
well-defined standard.

I think JSON is becoming easier to deal with on the command-line.  For
example, https://github.com/stedolan/jq has 6,713 stars on github.

(Also, how many *Stan users are dealing with output on the unix command
line? I don't think it's more than 5-10%)

> I’m fine with metadata and such being stored in JSON
> but having the samples in JSON and not a straight CSV
> would be very, very disruptive.

I tend to think it's CSV that's the problem. There's no standard and we
have to flatten arrays using yet another bespoke convention that is hard
to communicate (column-major? row-major?).

Space is certainly a consideration -- but we should solve that in a
different way. Compression maybe. JSON and some binary format would be
OK too. Certainly not JSON, CSV, *and* a binary format.

Best,

AR
